summary: This informational document surveys possible avenues for denial-of-service attacks on Internet systems, aiming to push protocol designers and operators toward more robust designs. It discusses partial remedies and how some remedies can open other weaknesses. It was later updated by RFC 8996.

plainLanguage.summary: A shop can be shut down by a crowd pushing in just to block the door. This lists the ways that happens online and how designers can make it harder.

questions: what is a denial of service attack
how do you mitigate dos attacks
subtitle: A survey of how Internet systems can be knocked out by overload, and which defenses help or backfire.

tldr.problem: Because the original Internet architecture was designed for a closed context, almost all Internet services are vulnerable to denial-of-service attacks of sufficient scale.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogues attack avenues against end-systems, routers, links, DNS and more, explains how attack amplifiers work, and lists mitigations in protocol design, network configuration and implementation, noting where a defense opens a new weakness.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational survey meant to push designers toward more robust systems, not a protocol. It was later updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4732 is an Informational survey, not a standard, and it was updated by RFC 8996. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What Denial of Service Means
sections.content:
A denial-of-service (DoS) attack is one in which one or more machines target a victim and try to stop it doing useful work. The victim can be a server, client or router, a link, a whole network, a user, a company or an ISP. When the attack comes from many compromised hosts it is a distributed DoS (DDoS) attack.

The RFC says no consideration was given to DoS in the original Internet architecture, because of the closed context of the ARPANET and NSFNet, so almost all Internet services are vulnerable at sufficient scale. Its purposes are to show avenues for attack, to discuss partial solutions, and to show how partial solutions can be turned into other attacks, a recurrent theme that the authors say points to a lack of proper architectural solutions.

It also notes that a sufficiently subtle attack cannot in principle be told apart from a flash crowd, so defense is largely about raising the bar for malicious traffic, and not all DoS problems are malicious: failed links and misconfigured bots can cause overload too.
sections.plainLanguage: When the Internet was built, only a few trusted groups used it, so nobody planned for people trying to jam it. Now the goal is to make it hard to jam, since a huge honest crowd can look just like an attack.

sections.title: Attacks on End-Systems and Ongoing Connections
sections.content:
Attacks on end-systems range from crashing software through bugs, such as the 1996 "ping of death" (a fragmented ICMP echo request totalling more than the 65535 bytes allowed in an IPv4 packet), to exhausting resources such as memory, CPU, disk space, process counts or connection limits. Some resources renew themselves when the attack stops, others such as disk space do not. Limits set too low make the attacker's job easier, and limits set too high can allow a crash or livelock, where extra load reduces useful work.

Two classic TCP examples are the SYN-flood, which exhausts memory by leaving half-open connections, and the Ack-flood, which exhausts CPU because lookups for packets from never-established connections were inefficient. The RFC warns that strong authentication does not necessarily help: an expensive cryptographic check that must run before a packet can be discarded makes CPU exhaustion easier.

Protection mechanisms can be abused too. An attacker who knows a user ID can trigger a lockout after failed logins, or use up a hosting quota, or drive up a victim's traffic charges.

Ongoing communications can be attacked as well. An attacker who can observe a TCP connection can spoof packets to reset it or desynchronize it, and TLS or ssh do not prevent that because authentication happens after TCP has processed the packets. Predictable ports or initial sequence numbers make blind attacks feasible. Attackers can also make a victim overload itself, for instance by spoofing a UDP echo request so that an echo port and a chargen server bounce packets between them.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker can break a computer with a bad message, use up everything it has (like filling every chair in a waiting room), or trick it into locking out its own users. Honest-looking tricks like pretending to be a friend can also cut off a conversation.

sections.title: Attacks on Routers, Links and Infrastructure
sections.content:
Routers are end-systems too, so they can be flooded on their control ports. A stalled router can make routing protocols time out, causing churn. BGP route flap damping can even suppress legitimate flapping routes, making whole networks unreachable. Routing protocols can be abused with overloaded routing tables, route churn, spoofed desirable routes that draw traffic to the attacker, or inconsistent information that makes traffic loop. Configured route limits can backfire, because spoofed routes can push out legitimate ones.

Multicast adds more room for attack: Any-Source Multicast lets a sender create routing state in many routers, while Source-Specific Multicast prevents sender-based attacks on that state but still lets receivers join many groups. Inside a router, the link between the control processor and the forwarding engines, forwarding caches and automatically installed ACL entries can be overwhelmed.

Local networks have their own weak points: exhausting a DHCP address pool, answering DHCP or ARP before the legitimate party, broadcast storms, and 802.11 weaknesses such as unprotected association, spoofable SSIDs and forged deauthenticate or disassociate frames. Beacons cannot easily be encrypted because stations need them before authenticating.

Other targets include DNS (the 16-bit DNS ID is a limited defense against forged responses and anycast cuts both ways), links congested by non-congestion-controlled traffic, firewalls and intrusion detection systems (stateful firewalls can run out of memory, and a predictable hash function can degrade lookups from O(1) to O(n)), NTP, and even physical, social-engineering, legal and spam or black-hole-list attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Almost every part of the network can be jammed: the road signs (routers), the roads (links), the phone book (DNS), the security guards (firewalls) and the local Wi-Fi. Sometimes the easiest trick is simply to unplug something.

sections.title: Attack Amplifiers
sections.content:
An attack amplifier lets an attacker spoof the victim's source address so that other machines send larger responses to the victim. The RFC describes several kinds:

  • Smurf: an ICMP echo request with the victim's address is sent to a subnet-broadcast address, and every host replies to the victim. Today routers usually drop these and end-systems do not respond.
  • DNS reflection: a small spoofed query gets a much larger response, and the RFC notes that the largest DNS responses tend to be those carrying DNSSEC data.
  • Retransmission ("bang.c"): a spoofed TCP SYN makes many servers send SYN|ACK, then retransmit it several times when no final ACK arrives.
  • Relayed requests and payload addresses: a proxy that repeatedly retries toward a chosen victim, or a protocol such as SIP that carries a destination address in its payload, can be aimed at a victim. The "voice hammer" uses a SIP INVITE of a few hundred bytes to start a media stream of up to megabits per second, and needs no spoofing.

The lessons are to use ingress filtering to prevent source address spoofing, to avoid responses much larger than requests unless the client's address is validated with a handshake containing an unpredictable nonce, to have the client perform all retransmission during connection setup, to avoid proxies relaying to arbitrary destinations, and to validate any unavoidable third-party connections before sending significant data.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine someone writing your name and address on a thousand letters asking companies to send you their giant catalogues. They each send a big package to you after one tiny request. The cure is to check who really asked.

sections.title: Mitigation Strategies
sections.content:
The RFC first says provision for foreseeable peak load, since underprovisioned sites are the easiest to take down. Then it divides defense into avoiding attacks better than generic resource consumption, and limiting how much generic consumption crowds out legitimate users.

Protocol design. Do not hold state for unverified hosts, for example by using SYN cookies, at the server's discretion. Making it hard to simulate a legitimate user can use puzzles, reverse Turing tests or reachability testing, but each has limits, especially because bots give attackers plenty of computing power. Routing protocols should degrade gracefully under overload: RIP can drop a route it cannot store, while BGP must restart or shut down peerings. Unauthenticated autoconfiguration opens avenues for attack.

Network design. Provide private out-of-band access to control ports, avoid risky default settings such as IP redirect, directed broadcast and proxy ARP, spread service across redundant locations, authenticate routing adjacencies (for BGP, at least TCP MD5 or IPsec combined with GTSM), and isolate router-to-router traffic.

Router and end-system implementation. Check the syntax and semantics of routing messages, run consistency checks, tune operations such as prefix limits and BGP timers, and handle resource exhaustion carefully (for example, an ARP cache filling during a virus attack, or saturated queues between ASICs and the CPU). On end-systems, use state lookups an attacker cannot steer, such as keyed hash tables, avoid livelock, use unpredictable session identifiers, drop bad traffic early with ingress filtering, and set up monitoring before an attack happens.
sections.plainLanguage: To stay open when a crowd pushes in: have enough room for a busy day, make people prove they are real before you hold a seat for them, keep a back door for the staff, and write down what a normal day looks like so you notice trouble.

sections.title: Conclusions and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The conclusion restates that the document highlights possible avenues for DoS attacks to encourage more robust designs, that it discusses partial solutions, and that some of those can be exploited for other attacks. The focus is on protocol and network architecture, though operators can do much to lessen the threat.

The Security Considerations section is a single sentence: this entire document is about security.
sections.plainLanguage: The big idea is that you cannot stop every trick, but you can make jamming costly and avoid fixes that create new holes.
